paras.text: In polluted areas, the concentrations of these acids can be much higher and can reduce the pH of rain water substantially. In particular, acid rain is a serious problem for areas located near the coal-fired power plants. Heavy metals e.g. Cu, Hg and Pb are also dissolved by acid rain producing various toxic effects.

23.2 Chemistry of the Stratosphere

As mentioned earlier in this unit (Table 23.1) stratosphere is the part of atmosphere which extends from 11–50 km above the Earth’s surface. The temperature of the stratosphere ranges from –56°C to –2°C. The important chemical species that exists in this sphere is ozone (O₃), which acts as a protective shield (layer) for the survival of life on the Earth from the harmful effects of sun’s UV radiations. The temperature of this sphere increases with increasing altitude.

Production and Destruction of Ozone

The production of ozone in the stratosphere results from the breaking of the chemical bond of oxygen molecule (O₂) by high energy solar radiations (UV radiations). This process, called photo dissociation, results in the release of single oxygen atoms.

The oxygen atoms produced in the reaction, then combine with oxygen molecules to form ozone.

Conditions most suitable for ozone formation are found at intermediate altitude (between 25 and 30 km where both oxygen molecules and free oxygen atoms are present.) Ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs UV radiations from the sun and does not allow them to reach the Earth’s surface thus it protects us from the harmful effects of these radiations.

Ozone is also destroyed by solar radiation. When O₃ absorbs a solar UV photons it dissociates into O₂ and O.

Also, when O₃ encounters a free oxygen atom (O), the two can combine to form two O₂ molecules.

The concentration of O₃ depends on the relative rates of the formation and destruction reactions.

… (NOₓ), emitted into the atmosphere react with water, oxygen, and other chemicals to form sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) and nitric acid (HNO₃). These, then, mix with water and fall on the ground in the form of acid rain. A small portion of the SO₂ and NOₓ that cause acid rain is from natural sources such as volcanos and NO produced in lightening and forest fires, but most of them come from the burning of fossil fuels and other human activities.

In polluted areas, the concentrations of these acids can be much higher and can reduce the pH of rain water substantially. Acid rain can fall quite far from the sources of pollution, due to long-range atmospheric transport by wind and air currents. In particular, acid rain is a serious problem for areas located near the coal-fired power plants. Acid rain, on one hand, is a serious threat to the human life as it contaminates the drinking water and on the other hand is a problem for plants, animals, aquatic life, and building material. Heavy metals e.g. Cu, Hg and Pb are also dissolved by acid rain producing various toxic effects.

Acidic streams and lakes or rivers affect the aquatic life. High acidity may result in killing of fish, reduces their growth and causes reproductive failure. Hatching of fish eggs is prevented due to change in pH of water. Moreover, green algae and many forms of beneficial bacteria, which are essential to aquatic life are also killed as a result of acidity in water. Plant growth is seriously inhibited due to acid rain. In addition, the acid rain also corrodes buildings, monuments, statues, and metals. For example, H₂SO₄ destroys the CaCO₃ of the building material according to the following reaction.

23.2 Chemistry of the Stratosphere

As mentioned earlier in this unit (Table 23.1) stratosphere is the part of atmosphere which extends from 11–50 km above the Earth’s surface. The temperature of the stratosphere ranges from –56°C to –2°C. The important chemical species that exists in this sphere is ozone (O₃), which acts as a protective shield (layer) for the survival of life on the Earth from the harmful effects of sun’s UV radiations. The temperature of this sphere increases with increasing altitude.

Production and Destruction of Ozone

The production of ozone in the stratosphere results from the breaking of the chemical bond of oxygen molecule (O₂) by high energy solar radiations (UV radiations). This process, called photo dissociation, results in the release of single oxygen atoms.

The oxygen atoms produced in the reaction, then combine with oxygen molecules to form ozone.

Conditions most suitable for ozone formation are found at intermediate altitude (between 25 and 30 km where both oxygen molecules and free oxygen atoms are present.) Ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs UV radiations from the sun and does not allow them to reach the Earth’s surface thus it protects us from the harmful effects of these radiations.

Ozone is also destroyed by solar radiation. When O₃ absorbs a solar UV photons it dissociates into O₂ and O.

Also, when O₃ encounters a free oxygen atom (O), the two can combine to form two O₂ molecules.

The concentration of O₃ depends on the relative rates of the formation and destruction reactions.
